counterexample: Axiom AX. Lemma L1 cites only AX and claims P; its derivation text reads 'since Q holds, P follows'. Lemma L2 cites L1 and claims Q, derived from P. Declared premise graph: AX -> L1 -> L2, strictly directed and acyclic, so the axiom's requirement is met and any mechanical DAG check passes. The reasoning is nonetheless circular: P rests on Q and Q rests on P. Nothing mechanical prevents it prior to LLM verification; it is the LLM entailment probe on L1 ('assumes Q, which it does not cite') that would catch it, after the mechanical check has already passed.
reasoning: Attacked the phrase 'circular reasoning': a DAG check sees declared premise edges only, while circularity can live in the statements. The scenario satisfies the sole premise (the declared graph is strictly directed and acyclic) and the claim as written fails: the circular reasoning is not prevented mechanically and reaches the LLM verifier unflagged, where it can only surface as an uncited-assumption gap. The claim survives only under the narrower restatement 'prevents cycles among declared premise edges', which is the author's move.

counterexample: A premise that every mutation of the premise graph (load from the committed declaration, proposal, restatement) is gated by a cycle check that rejects on failure; that no verification trial is accepted against a node whose premise edges have not passed that check; and that 'circular reasoning' means a cycle in declared premise edges.
reasoning: The premise is a norm ('must be acyclic'); it supplies neither a mechanism nor a schedule. Structural induction on directed graph insertion yields at most 'a graph built solely by checked single-edge insertions stays acyclic', and only if (a) a rejecting check exists, (b) every mutation path goes through it -- initial load from the committed declaration, staged proposals, and restatement of a node's premise list (a replacement, not an insertion) -- and (c) verification is withheld until the check has passed. None of (a)-(c) is stated. The clause 'prior to any LLM semantic verification attempt' is a claim about scheduling relative to verification, which induction on the graph cannot reach: the rule never mentions verification. Also unstated: that 'circular reasoning' is coextensive with a cycle in declared edges.

From 'deductive reasoning graphs must be strictly directed and acyclic' one derives, with equal force, a design that enforces the norm by semantic review -- verifiers flag a citation chain that returns to itself, and the mechanical check runs only at commit, after verification -- and a design that gates mechanically first. Both satisfy the axiom. So NOT(claim) ('mechanical checking does not precede LLM verification' / 'some circular reasoning is not prevented mechanically') is as derivable from the premise as the claim; the premise decides neither the existence of the mechanical gate nor its ordering.

Strongest attacks: (1) Prune or rename the cited premise. The child's citation no longer resolves, so a traversal over resolving dependency edges gives the child in-degree 0, emits it as a root, and nothing propagates to it; both premises hold (the graph stays acyclic; a deletion is a modification) and the child is unmarked. It does not falsify: a design consistent with the premises can resolve a dangling citation to a synthetic 'missing' node treated as modified, and the traversal then reaches the child, so the outcome hinges on a design choice the premises do not fix -- carried as the entailment gap. (2) A cycle in the traversed graph: Kahn's traversal never emits the cycle's members or anything downstream of them, so they are silently unmarked -- but that scenario violates AXM-acyclicity and refutes nothing. (3) A node whose derivation text presupposes the modified node without citing it: affected in substance, but not a 'child' over dependency edges, so outside the claim's wording. (4) Re-verify the direct child after the upstream change and ask whether the grandchild stays marked: on the claim's wording ('identified and marked') the grandchild was marked at traversal time, so the claim as written survives; persistence is the axiom's 'until re-verified', which the claim does not carry.

counterexample: A premise that the graph the traversal runs on is in fact acyclic, and that every premise citation of every node in scope (declared or staged; axiom, definition, policy, lemma or branch) is a resolving dependency edge in that traversal, re-run after each modification, with STALE persisting until re-verification.
reasoning: Kahn topological traversal yields reachability-complete marking only on the graph it is handed. The claim needs, and the rule does not supply: (a) that the traversed graph is in fact acyclic -- AXM-acyclicity is a norm ('must be'), and this lemma does not cite any enforcement lemma; on a graph where the norm is violated the traversal silently skips the cycle and everything downstream of it; (b) that 'dependency edges' comprise every premise citation of every node in scope -- axiom, definition, policy, lemma, branch; declared at the committed revision or staged in the ledger -- and that each citation resolves (a pruned or renamed premise leaves a dangling citation the traversal cannot follow); (c) that the traversal is re-run after every modification and that 'modified' is detectable per node; (d) that a STALE mark persists until that node is re-verified, which the axiom's 'until re-verified' requires but the claim's 'identified and marked' does not carry. Whether (a)-(d) hold can only be judged from the implementation.

The premises fix the effect -- downstream derived conclusions are invalid until re-verified -- and nothing about the mechanism. A design that satisfies both axioms with no STALE mark and no traversal at all (each verdict recomputed at read time from the statement set its trials were bound to, so an upstream restatement simply returns the node to unproven) derives NOT(claim) -- 'topological ordering identifies and marks nothing' -- with the same standing as the claim. The premises decide the effect, not the claim as worded.

Attacks tried: (1) A record whose provenance label is 'asserted' but which originated from a server-run test, with belief keyed on origin rather than label: fails because DEF-belief-eligible equates each label with its origin ('measured (the server ran the declared test and captured the artifact)'), so a server-run record carrying 'asserted' contradicts the definition -- the scenario violates a premise. (2) Reclassifying an asserted record as measured after the fact: the record that then changes belief no longer has provenance asserted, and if it changes belief without the server having run the declared test the design violates AXM-no-belief-write-path; either way not every premise holds. (3) A note that retracts or supersedes a measured record: a statement changing belief, which the axiom's zero-weight clause forbids. (4) A note that prompts a human to run a test whose result changes belief: the belief changes through the measured evidence, not through the note -- 'through' is the axiom's relation and the claim's. (5) A trial record (not a note) that an agent reports with provenance asserted: excluded by the definition's 'eligible = measured or imported' and by the axiom's zero weight. No scenario satisfies both premises and defeats the claim.

The step is modus tollens: AXM-no-belief-write-path states a necessary condition for any belief change (evidence the server produced by a declared test, or imported with an artifact and its hash); DEF-belief-eligible ties each provenance label to its origin and places asserted outside both; so an asserted record cannot be the channel of any change. Checked what the step leans on: that the label reflects the origin -- supplied by the definition's parentheticals, not by an implementation fact; that 'belief slice' is a part of the belief the axiom governs -- carried by the term itself; that 'cannot change' means 'is not the channel of change' -- the axiom's own 'through'. Nothing further is assumed.

NOT(claim) -- some asserted record changes a belief slice -- would require a belief to change through a statement by an agent or a human, which the axiom's second clause denies outright ('carries zero weight'). It is not derivable from the premises; the premises decide the claim rather than merely permit it.

Strongest attacks: (1) An uncommitted edit to a declaration file dirties the working tree, and a design that judges evidence staleness or the basis hash against the working tree's state rather than the committed revision flips verdicts to stale: the axiom holds on its natural reading (the edit's content takes no effect) and the claim fails. It does not falsify: whether any verdict reads the working tree by a non-content channel is a design choice the premise does not fix, so it is carried as the entailment gap. (2) The server caching the working-tree copy of the declaration at startup: gives the uncommitted content effect, which violates the axiom. (3) A commit made by an agent rather than a human: the edit is then committed, outside the claim's scope (noted separately as a weakness of the axiom). (4) A ledger proposal sharing the id of the uncommitted declaration: its verdict is a function of the ledger, which the file edit does not touch.

counterexample: A premise that a verdict and a proof state are functions of the declarations at the committed revision and the ledger only -- in particular that evidence staleness and the basis hash are computed from the committed revision, never from the working tree.
reasoning: The axiom gives that the edited content is not in effect. The derivation rule then adds 'a verdict and a proof state are functions of the declarations in effect and the ledger' -- the load-bearing clause -- and no cited premise supplies it: AXM-commit-is-approval says nothing about what verdicts are functions of, and 'the working tree is inert until a human commits it' reads naturally as the declaration edit being inert, not as a guarantee that no verdict reads the working tree by another channel (evidence staleness judged against a dirty tree; a basis hash computed over the file on disk). That clause can only be judged from the implementation.

NOT(claim) -- some uncommitted declaration edit changes a verdict or proof state -- can only be reached by positing a channel from the working tree that the axiom neither names nor licenses, while the axiom's inertness clause pushes the other way. NOT(claim) is not derivable; the premise favours the claim and is merely silent on non-content channels (the gap), not symmetric.

subject: LMA-blast-radius-propagation
text: Noticed, not turned into a trial: this lemma cites AXM-acyclicity (a norm) but not LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity, so its acyclicity-in-fact is unbacked by any lemma -- and the enforcement lemma is now refuted on its wording. Kahn traversal on a graph that violates the norm terminates without emitting the cycle's members or anything downstream of them, i.e. the failure mode is silent under-marking rather than an error. If the author restates the enforcement lemma to 'rejects any premise edge that would close a cycle among declared edges, before any trial is offered on the node', this lemma should cite it. Also: 'every affected child ... marked STALE' does not carry the axiom's 'until re-verified'; a persistence clause would let downstream branches lean on it.

subject: LMA-asserted-is-inert
text: Noticed, not turned into a trial (outside this lemma's wording): in the consistency ledger a verification trial is itself a statement by an agent, yet it moves proof state (PROVEN/REFUTED), and independence is counted from an agent-supplied actor label. Whichever node squares that with AXM-no-belief-write-path ('a statement by an agent or a human carries zero weight') should say whether a recorded probe counts as evidence the server produced, and what stops one agent from manufacturing independence by varying its actor label. A second, softer point: 'imported (brought in with a source, an artifact and its hash)' admits an artifact that is itself an agent's assertion, hashed; the hash proves integrity, not measurement.

subject: LMA-worktree-inert
text: Noticed, not turned into a trial (outside the claim's scope): AXM-commit-is-approval says a declaration takes effect 'from the committed revision' and the working tree is inert 'until a human commits it'. A commit made by an agent satisfies the first clause and not the second, and nothing in the premises lets the server tell the two apart; if commit is to mean human approval, the axiom needs either a premise that only humans commit or a channel that distinguishes an approved commit. This is the author's call; the lemma as written is untouched by it.

reasoning: I looked for a scenario where the axiom holds and the claimed behaviour itself fails, and found none. The axiom only restricts: a recommendation to optimise needs an observation of its target against the target's own contract, and an end-to-end outcome alone attributes to no component. Everything the claim prescribes either holds something back (no optimisation, no blame) or recommends something that optimises nothing (instrument). So no scenario that satisfies the premise can make the prescribed behaviour break it. Attacks tried: (a) Leader A leads by prior and no declared test observes it. A declared test observes B against B's own contract and B fails. The claimed design holds back on B and names instrumentation, which complies with the axiom. A diagnosis that recommends optimising B would also comply. That shows the claim is under-determined (see entailment and negation), not that it is false. (b) A has no contract of its own, so instrumentation alone cannot produce the observation the axiom asks for. Naming instrumentation is still neither an optimisation nor a blame, so the claim holds as stated. (c) A is itself the layer that does the observing, so 'instrument' might read as optimising an unobserved A. This fails: adding a test that observes A does not change A. (d) Self-contradiction: if being the leading candidate counted as blame, an unobserved leader would break the claim's own last clause. This fails because the claim separates naming a leader to instrument from blaming it, and no premise makes being a candidate an attribution. (e) An observation of A against its own contract exists outside any declared test. The claim still holds back optimisation and names instrumentation. That is overly cautious but complies. It exposes a mismatch between 'declared test' and 'observation', which I record as a gap, not as a falsity.

counterexample: Beyond AXM-observe-before-optimise, the claim needs four premises and two definitions. (1) Completeness: a diagnosis always names exactly one binding constraint, and when the leading candidate has no observation against its own contract, that constraint is the missing observation. (2) Observation: an observation of a component against its own contract comes only from a declared test that targets that contract, and every candidate has a contract of its own. (3) Scope: while the leading candidate is unobserved, no other component may be recommended for optimisation. (4) Blame: only an observation against a component's own contract attributes a failure to it (strengthening the axiom's 'end-to-end outcome alone'), or a definition that makes 'blame' mean 'recommend for optimisation'. Definitions: 'leading candidate' and 'binding constraint'.
reasoning: The axiom decides two things. No component may be recommended for optimisation without an observation of it against its own contract. No failure may be attributed from an end-to-end outcome alone. The claim adds clauses the axiom does not reach. (1) 'Names instrumentation as the binding constraint': the axiom never requires a recommendation. The derivation's step 'the only recommendation that satisfies the axiom is to instrument' is false, because two other responses satisfy it equally: reporting 'insufficient' and naming nothing, or recommending optimisation of another component observed against its own contract. Whether the diagnosis names instrumentation is a fact about its behaviour that no premise fixes. (2) The unqualified 'recommends no optimisation': the axiom requires an observation only of the target, and a passing observation counts as much as a failing one, so any other observed component may be recommended. (3) 'No declared test observes': the axiom's condition is 'no observation against its own contract'. The two come apart when an observation comes from outside the declared tests, or when a declared test observes the component against some other contract. (4) 'Blamed only on an observation against its own contract': the axiom excludes only an end-to-end outcome ALONE. That leaves attribution by elimination open: an end-to-end failure with every other component observed passing its own contract. (5) 'Leading candidate' and 'binding constraint' are undefined in the premises. The cited evidence contract bears on whether the diagnosis behaves this way, not on whether the claim follows. It is not a premise and cannot close the gap.

The part of the claim the axiom decides cannot be negated from it. Recommending optimisation of the unobserved leader, or attributing a failure from an end-to-end outcome alone, would contradict the axiom. The rest of the claim can be negated. A mirror derivation from the same axiom: an optimisation recommendation needs an observation of its target and nothing more. So suppose leader A is observed by no declared test, but a declared test has observed B against B's own contract. A diagnosis that recommends optimising B, and names B's contract result rather than instrumentation as the binding constraint, satisfies the axiom exactly as well as the claimed design does. The axiom excludes attribution only from an end-to-end outcome ALONE, so attributing the failure to A after every other component has been observed passing its own contract is not excluded either. On three clauses the axiom supports NOT(claim) as well as the claim: 'names instrumentation as the binding constraint', the unqualified 'recommends no optimisation', and 'blamed only on an observation against its own contract'. The premises are too weak to decide the claim as written.

counterexample: Start from the empty graph. (1) Admit A citing nothing. (2) Admit B citing A: A is a different node, already in the graph, and does not depend on B; edge A->B. (3) A leaves the graph (its declaration is removed; no hypothesis restricts removal); B stays and still cites A, which with A absent is no edge, so the graph is {B} with no edges. (4) Admit A again, now citing B: B is a different node, already in the graph, and does not depend on A (A is absent, so no path leads from it to B); admitted. By DEF-premise-graph the graph now holds B->A (A cites B) and A->B (B cites A): a cycle. The build began empty, every edge was added at an admission (A->B at steps 2 and 4, B->A at step 4), and every admission passed the stated check. The same cycle forms with no removal at all if B enters as a declared or staged node citing A before A exists, since the stated check governs admission only; A is then admitted citing B.
reasoning: Attacked the induction step 'each new edge runs from some p in P to n'. DEF-premise-graph makes the edges a function of citations among the nodes present ('an edge from each premise a node cites to that node'), so admitting n creates, besides the edges from its own premises, an edge n->m for every node m already in the graph that cites n. The third hypothesis only guarantees n was present at the moment m was admitted; neither the claim nor the definition keeps n present afterwards, and neither requires every node to enter by admission (the definition lists declared and staged nodes beside admitted ones). Once some m in the graph holds a citation of an absent n, admitting n citing m passes the stated check vacuously -- no path leads from a node that is not in the graph -- and closes a cycle. Attacks that failed: a self-loop is excluded by 'a different node'; restating a node that is present is caught, as the derivation says, because its outgoing edges are in the graph when the dependence check runs.

counterexample: The claim needs a hypothesis that no node in the graph ever cites a node absent from it -- every node enters the graph by admission, and a node leaves only together with every node that cites it -- so that admitting n adds only edges into n from the premises n cites; and that admissions are applied one at a time, each checked against the graph the previous one left.
reasoning: The induction holds only if admitting n adds no edge out of n. The claim's second hypothesis says every edge is added by admitting a node; it does not say that the edges an admission adds all run into the admitted node, and DEF-premise-graph, which derives edges from citations, implies the opposite whenever some node in the graph already cites n. The derivation supplies this step ('Each new edge runs from some p in P to n') without a premise for it. A second step is also assumed without being stated: that admissions happen one at a time. 'Induction on admissions' needs each admission checked against a graph holding every earlier admission's edges. Suppose two restatements, A citing B and B citing A, are each checked against the same edgeless state and applied together. Each passes the stated check, and together they form a cycle.

The premises are silent on whether a node may leave the graph, or enter it without admission, while another node cites it, and on whether admissions are serialized. Where none of these occurs, the induction in the derivation goes through and the claim follows. Where any one occurs, the construction in the counterexample trial satisfies all three hypotheses and DEF-premise-graph and yields a cycle, so NOT(claim) is derivable from the same premises. As written, the premises do not decide the claim.

counterexample: Lemma r cites axiom q, and nothing cites r, so AXM-blast-radius-invalidation has no downstream conclusion to invalidate. The kernel counts a trial exactly while its target is in the graph and every fingerprint it recorded matches, which meets the third hypothesis. (1) r has statement S1; trial T1 of r records fp(r)=F1 and fp(q). (2) r is restated to S2; fp(r)=F2 differs from F1, and T1 stops counting. (3) r is restated back to S1, citing q as before. By the first hypothesis fp(r) is F1 again, and fp(q) has not changed. T1's target is in the graph and every fingerprint it recorded matches, so T1 counts. T1 is an earlier trial of r; restating r did not stop it from counting but restored it, with no re-verification. The claim that restating a node stops every earlier trial of it from counting fails. Under the literal necessary-only reading of the third hypothesis, the second conclusion also fails. Take a kernel that stops every trial recorded before any restatement, wherever that trial's target sits; it meets every hypothesis. Restating r then stops the trials of a node e that does not depend on r, although the claim says they keep counting as before.
reasoning: Attacked the derivation's step 'Every earlier trial of r recorded the old one'. By the first hypothesis a node's fingerprint is a function of its statement and the premises it cites and nothing else, so a restatement that restores an earlier statement restores the earlier fingerprint, and the trials recorded under that statement match again. The third hypothesis ('counts only while') gives only a necessary condition, so a kernel that counts a trial whenever its target is in the graph and its recorded fingerprints match satisfies it -- and the derivation itself reads it that way ('a trial recorded afterwards carries the new fingerprints and counts'). Under that kernel the restatement revives earlier trials instead of stopping them. Second attack, on the conclusion that other nodes' trials keep counting: since the third and fourth hypotheses are necessary conditions only, a kernel that on any restatement stops every trial recorded before it, anywhere in the graph, satisfies all four hypotheses and AXM-blast-radius-invalidation (which demands invalidation downstream and forbids none elsewhere), yet stops the trials of a node that does not depend on the restated one. Attacks that failed: a dependency acquired after a trial was recorded always changes the fingerprint of the target or of an ancestor that trial recorded, because by the fourth hypothesis no node in the graph cites a node absent from it, so a new path can only arrive through a changed citation; the removal half follows from the fourth hypothesis by induction on path length, with or without cycles; restating r cannot create a new path out of r, so the set of nodes independent of r is the same before and after.

counterexample: The claim needs three things. First: a trial counts exactly while (if and only if) its target is in the graph and every fingerprint it recorded matches. Second: a node leaves the graph only when it is removed or a premise it cites leaves. Third, one of: a fingerprint that never recurs across restatements of a node (it changes on every restatement, not only as a function of content), or a first conclusion limited to earlier trials whose recorded fingerprints differ from the current ones.
reasoning: Three steps in the derivation go beyond the hypotheses as written. (a) Two inferences draw counting from the conditions of the third hypothesis: 'a trial recorded afterwards ... counts' and 'e's trials count as before'. That hypothesis states the conditions only as necessary ('counts only while'); nothing says a trial that meets them counts. (b) 'every node that leaves the graph is r or depends on r' treats the fourth hypothesis ('stays only while every premise it cites does') as the only way a node leaves the graph; as stated, it permits other departures. (c) 'Every earlier trial of r recorded the old one' assumes no earlier trial recorded a fingerprint equal to the new one. With fingerprints determined by content, restoring an earlier statement restores the earlier fingerprint. Making (a) sufficient does not fix the claim, because the revival in (c) then follows. The revival also reaches a dependent d of r: a trial of d recorded while r had its earlier statement counts again once r is restored, with no re-verification after r's last modification. So under a biconditional counting rule, the mechanism does not deliver AXM-blast-radius-invalidation's 'until re-verified' in that case, which contradicts the derivation's closing sentence.

Read the third hypothesis as a biconditional, which is how the derivation uses it. Then the restoration scenario derives NOT(claim) outright: an earlier trial of the restated node counts after the restatement. Under the literal necessary-only reading, the premises do not decide the claim. Some admissible kernels satisfy both conclusions, for example one that also requires a trial to postdate the last restatement of every node whose fingerprint it recorded. Others violate one conclusion: the biconditional kernel violates the first, and a kernel that stops all earlier trials on any restatement violates the second. On neither reading is NOT(claim) excluded by the premises.

counterexample: The server runs a declared test on contract slice s, and the run's artifact is not captured. The record it keeps is not measured, because DEF-belief-eligible requires a captured artifact for that. It is not imported either, so it carries provenance asserted; the premises tie asserted to no particular origin and exclude no record from it. The record is still evidence the server itself produced by running a declared test, so AXM-no-belief-write-path allows the posterior over s to change through it, and the server updates the posterior with it. Every premise holds: the belief changed only through server-produced test evidence, no statement by an agent or a human carried weight, and the record is indeed not belief-eligible. Yet a record with provenance asserted changed a belief slice. The same happens with a record brought in with an artifact and its hash but no source: the axiom's second route admits it, and the definition's imported provenance does not.
reasoning: Attacked the derivation's step 'by DEF-belief-eligible an asserted record is neither'. DEF-belief-eligible says which records are belief-eligible; it never says an asserted record lies outside the two routes AXM-no-belief-write-path leaves open. Those routes are broader than the definition's provenances. The axiom's first route, evidence the server itself produced by running a declared test, does not require a captured artifact; measured provenance does. The second route, evidence imported with an artifact and its hash, does not require a source; imported provenance does. A record in that band is neither measured nor imported, so if provenance takes only the three values the definition names, it is asserted. The axiom still lets it change a posterior: 'changes only through' is a necessary condition, so it permits the change, and no premise makes belief-eligibility the condition for changing a belief. Attacks that failed: an agent's or a human's asserted statement that tries to add weight to, reweight or discard measured evidence is barred by the zero-weight clause and by 'only through'. An asserted record that merely prompts someone to run a test changes the belief only through the resulting test evidence, which the claim allows.

counterexample: The claim needs one of two premises. Either a measured belief changes only through belief-eligible evidence (every record the server produced by running a declared test, or imported with an artifact and its hash, has provenance measured or imported, never asserted). Or every record with provenance asserted is a statement by an agent or a human, which brings it under the axiom's zero-weight clause. It also needs every belief slice to be the posterior over a contract slice.
reasoning: The derivation moves from 'not belief-eligible', which is what DEF-belief-eligible gives, to 'not evidence the server produced or imported with an artifact', which is what AXM-no-belief-write-path needs. That move is valid only if every record on the axiom's routes is belief-eligible. The definition is stricter than the axiom (a captured artifact for measured, a source for imported), so the inference runs the wrong way. A second, smaller unstated step: the axiom speaks of 'a measured belief -- the posterior over a contract slice', while the claim speaks of 'any belief slice', and no premise says the two coincide.

The premises never say what provenance asserted covers. If asserted records are exactly statements by agents or humans, the axiom's zero-weight clause yields the claim directly. If a record in the band between the axiom's routes and the definition's provenances can carry asserted, as it must when provenance takes only the three named values, the scenario in the counterexample trial yields NOT(claim). The premises leave both open, so they do not decide the claim.

Tried each input the axiom names and each route around it. The head revision: an edit that is not committed, even one staged for commit, moves no revision, so the declarations at the head are unchanged. Commits that evidence names: an edit creates no commit, so the named commits hold what they held. A verdict or proof state that reports the working tree's state, such as a flag for uncommitted changes, would be computed from a working-tree file other than the ledger, which the axiom forbids. Inputs that are not files, such as time, can change outputs, but not because of the edit. The strongest attacks went through the ledger, the one working-tree input the axiom admits. (a) A file that holds declarations and is also the ledger. An uncommitted edit to its ledger part changes the proof state, and this breaks neither sentence of the axiom, since the file's declarations are still read from the committed revision. But the axiom names declarations and the ledger as distinct inputs, so I record their disjointness as an unstated premise, not as a refutation. (b) A declared test that checks declaration files, run in a working tree that carries a breaking edit. Its evidence names the head revision but reflects the edit, and every verdict computed from the ledger then depends on the edit. Here the change arrives through a later write to the ledger, not through the edit. I read the claim's subject as the edit itself, as the derivation does, so (b) is recorded as the entailment gap and not as a counterexample.

counterexample: The claim needs (i) a premise that no declaration file is, or contains, the ledger. For 'changes no verdict and no proof state' to cover more than the moment of the edit, it also needs (ii) a premise that no ledger entry is derived from uncommitted working-tree content. For example: evidence is produced only from the content of the commit it names, and a trial only from committed declarations and the ledger. Alternatively, the claim should be narrowed to the edit alone, with no later ledger write that depends on it.
reasoning: The derivation holds for the edit's own writes: the edit moves no revision and, if the declaration file is not the ledger, writes nothing to it, so every input is what it was. Two things it relies on are not in the premise. First, that no declaration file is, or holds, the ledger: the premise names the two as separate inputs but never says they are separate files. Second, and more important for a lemma about an inert working tree: the axiom makes the ledger an input read from the working tree, but says nothing about where ledger entries come from. Suppose an entry is produced from uncommitted content, such as evidence from a declared test run in a working tree that carries the edit and recorded against the head revision, or a trial whose author read the edited file. Then verdicts and proof states are functions of the edit even though no input changed at the moment it was made. The axiom's 'computed from the commits that evidence names' protects them only if evidence is faithful to the commit it names, and the premise does not state that.

The premise is silent on where ledger entries come from, and on whether a declaration file may also be the ledger. Under the reading the lemma's purpose suggests -- no verdict or proof state depends on uncommitted declaration content -- NOT(claim) follows from the same premise. Evidence from a declared test run in a working tree carrying the edit is recorded against the head revision, and every verdict computed from the ledger then depends on the edit; nothing in the axiom excludes this. Under the narrower reading -- the edit's own writes -- the premise yields the claim only once declaration files and the ledger are disjoint, which it does not state. Either way the premise alone does not decide the claim.

Attacks tried, all under DEF-premise-graph. (a) Self-citation: n cites n. Admission requires n already in the graph, but nodes enter only by admission and each at most once, so n is never admitted and the self-loop n->n is never added. (b) Two-node mutual citation a cites b, b cites a: whichever is considered first needs the other already present, so neither is ever admitted; the build ends with both left out, which is a legitimate end state (each left-out node cites a premise not in the graph). (c) Late back-edge: after a and b (b cites a) are admitted, could an edge b->a appear? Only an admission adds edges, and every edge added at an admission of m ends at m; a is never admitted again (at most once), so no edge into a is added after a's admission. (d) Same id declared at head and staged in the ledger with different citations: the definition ties the admission test and the added edges to the same 'premises it cites' of the one node, so the edges still all come from nodes already present. (e) Reading 'cycle' as an undirected cycle (diamond a->b, a->c, b->d, c->d): rejected, the definition fixes a directed graph and cycles among its directed edges. In every scenario that satisfies the premises, admission order is a topological order, so no directed cycle exists.

Every step of the derivation is supplied by DEF-premise-graph: start from the empty graph (base case acyclic); one node at a time, each at most once, nothing removed; a node is admitted only when every cited premise is already present; admission adds the node plus edges premise->node only; no other step adds nodes or edges. Hence every edge goes from an earlier admission to a later one, which rules out any directed cycle, including self-loops (a self-citing node can never meet its own admission condition). Termination and the end condition are irrelevant to acyclicity, which holds at every intermediate stage and so for any build. The lemma disclaims uncited assumptions, and the definition itself says those are not edges, so no clause of the claim needs a fact the definition does not declare.

NOT(claim) means some build contains a directed cycle. Since the definition makes admission order a strict order that every edge respects, this could only be derived if the definition were self-contradictory. I checked: 'admitted only once every premise it cites is already in the graph' and 'ends only when every node left out cites a premise that is not in it' are jointly satisfiable (cyclic or dangling citers are simply left out), and nothing in the definition allows removal, re-admission, or edge insertion outside admission. So the negation is not derivable, and the premises settle the claim.

counterexample: Declarations: axiom A; lemma r with statement S1 citing A; lemma e citing r. Trial T of e is valid and recorded fingerprints fp(e), fp(r)=F(S1,{A}), fp(A) while all three were in the graph, so T is current. Restatement 1: r is restated to S2 citing A and Q, and Q is declared nowhere. No build admits r, so none admits e. After this restatement no edge reaches e, so by DEF-premise-graph e depends on nothing. T goes from current to not current. Read 'depends on r' in the build after the restatement and e is an 'other node', so clause (3) fails. Restatement 2: r is restated back to S1 citing A. Both r and e are admitted again. Fingerprints are determined by statement and cited premises, so fp(r) is F(S1,{A}) again. T is valid, its target is in the graph, and its recorded fingerprints equal the present ones, so T is current again. In the build before this restatement e was not in the graph and depended on nothing. Read 'depends on r' in the build before and e is an 'other node' whose trial changed, so clause (3) fails again. Every premise holds. DEF-premise-graph leaves out a node that cites a premise not in the graph. DEF-current-trial decides T's currentness at each step. The axiom's invalidation holds at restatement 1, and at restatement 2 T recorded exactly the content e and r now have. Under either single-build reading of 'depends on r' the claim fails.
reasoning: Clauses (1) and (2) survive. (1): under DEF-current-trial a fingerprinted trial is current only if its recorded fingerprints of its target and that target's then-dependencies match, node for node, the ones those nodes have now. A recorded fingerprint of r that differs from r's new one fails that match, whether or not r is still a dependency. (2): once r is removed, no build admits it, and induction along any before-removal path r->n1->...->e shows each ni is left out, so their trials are not current. Removal only shrinks the admitted set, so no other node's currentness changes. Clause (3) fails for restatement because DEF-premise-graph makes 'depends on' a matter of edges in one build, and a restatement can change the premises r cites. That moves r, and every node that cites r, into or out of the graph. The derivation's step 'e keeps its place in the graph' is where it breaks: it does not hold for a node that depends on r in only one of the two builds.

counterexample: Missing premise: 'depends on r' is evaluated over the union of the builds before and after the change (equivalently: over declared citation paths, whether or not the nodes are admitted); or: restating a node never changes the premises it cites.
reasoning: Clauses (1) and (2) follow from DEF-current-trial and DEF-premise-graph. Clause (3) needs a fact neither premise supplies. It is true only if 'depends on r' covers every node that depends on r in either the build before or the build after the change. Equivalently, it must cover every node whose declared citations lead back to r. Or a restatement must leave unchanged the premises r cites, so that r's admission, and with it the graph, cannot change. DEF-premise-graph defines dependence only within a single build. DEF-current-trial expressly lets a node's cited premises change ('differs whenever either differs'). So the step 'e keeps its place in the graph' is unsupported. The word 'removed' is also undefined. The derivation reads it as 'no longer declared at head nor staged in the ledger', which is the reading clause (2) needs.

Under the union reading of 'depends on r' (before or after, or declared citation ancestry), clause (3) is derivable. Nodes outside r's ancestry in both builds keep their admission, their dependencies and their fingerprints. Under either single-build reading, which is the only kind of dependence DEF-premise-graph defines, the premises let a restatement that changes r's citations change a non-dependent's currentness. That makes NOT(claim) derivable (see the counterexample trial). The premises do not fix which build 'depends on r' refers to, so they do not decide the claim as worded.

Attacks tried. (a) Mislabelled record: an agent writes a record tagged 'measured' but without a server run or artifact. By DEF-belief-eligible, provenance measured means the server ran a declared test and took metrics from the captured, hashed artifact. This record is neither measured nor imported, so it is asserted and not eligible. It changes nothing. (b) Asserted retraction: an asserted record marks a measured record invalid, and the posterior moves. The posterior would then have changed through a non-eligible record, which AXM-no-belief-write-path forbids, so the scenario violates a premise. Nor can an asserted record change another record's eligibility: DEF-belief-eligible makes eligibility depend only on that record's own provenance and on which contracts declared tests can measure. Neither is set by a record. (c) Provenance upgrade: an asserted record later gains an artifact and becomes imported. Provenance as defined describes how a record was made, and a record carries exactly one. Once it counts, the counting record is imported, not asserted. (d) Laundering: an agent turns a note into an artifact, hashes it and imports it. The record that moves the belief then has provenance imported, not asserted, so this claim is not violated. Whether that import fits the axiom's 'zero weight for a statement by an agent' is a question for the axiom and definition, not for this lemma. (e) A note prompts someone to run a declared test: the belief then changes through the measured record, not the note. No scenario that satisfies both premises lets an asserted record change a measured belief.

Two steps, each cited. DEF-belief-eligible: every record carries exactly one provenance, so an asserted record is neither measured nor imported and therefore not belief-eligible, whatever contract it targets. AXM-no-belief-write-path: a measured belief changes only through belief-eligible evidence. So no measured belief changes through an asserted record. The claim's 'cannot change' has to be read as the axiom's 'changes through'. Indirect influence that works by producing a separate eligible record is a change through that record, and neither premise attributes it to the asserted one. No other fact is needed.

NOT(claim): some asserted record changes a measured belief. With the axiom, that requires the asserted record to be belief-eligible. The definition's 'exactly one provenance' plus eligibility only for measured or imported records rules this out, so NOT(claim) could follow only from contradictory premises. The two are consistent: a three-valued provenance, the rule that anything else counts as asserted, and a write path open only to measured or imported records. The premises decide the claim.

Attacks tried. (a) Rewrite the declaration file by checking out or hard-resetting to another revision, with no commit. Verdicts change, but because the head revision moved, and by AXM-commit-is-approval the head revision is an input. That is not an uncommitted edit with head fixed, which is what the claim addresses. The edit's own contribution is nil. (b) Make a run's captured artifact a reference to the working-tree declaration file, so editing the file edits a ledger artifact. That would make the declaration file part of the ledger, which DEF-ledger excludes, so the scenario breaks a premise. (c) Evidence names a commit and the edit alters that commit's content: commits are fixed, and the edit makes none. (d) A server notices the dirty file and appends an event to the ledger that shifts a proof state. That is a separate later act by the server, not the edit, and the lemma scopes later acts out. If such an event carried the uncommitted content into a verdict, the declaration would take effect before commit, contrary to the axiom's first sentence. (e) An edit that adds a new untracked declaration file is equally outside head and outside the ledger. With head fixed, named commits unchanged and the ledger untouched, every input the axiom allows is unchanged, so no verdict or proof state changes.

AXM-commit-is-approval lists the only inputs to every verdict and proof state: declarations at the head revision, the commits evidence names, and the ledger. It excludes every other working-tree file. An uncommitted edit changes the contents of one working-tree file. It makes no commit, so head and the named commits are unchanged. By DEF-ledger the declaration file is not part of the ledger, so changing it changes no ledger record. Every input is therefore as it was, and the outputs are too. The only presupposition is the ordinary meaning of an uncommitted edit: the head revision stays where it was. The axiom's own contrast between committed revision and working tree supplies that, so no further premise is needed. Later acts (a commit, a run's evidence, any record a server appends) are expressly outside the claim.

NOT(claim) would need some uncommitted edit to a declaration file to change a verdict or proof state. The premises offer no channel for it. The file is neither committed content nor ledger, and the axiom bars every other working-tree file as an input and lets a declaration take effect only from the committed revision. No premise forces an edit to change any input, and the two premises are mutually consistent, so NOT(claim) is not derivable and the premises decide the claim.
